items.t: Type 2 diabetes mellitus, particularly in overweight patients, when diet and exercise alone do not give adequate glycaemic control. Adults: monotherapy, with other oral antidiabetics or with insulin. Children from 10 years: monotherapy or with insulin.

src.q: Treatment of type 2 diabetes mellitus, particularly in overweight patients, when dietary management and exercise alone does not result in adequate glycaemic control.
In children from 10 years of age and adolescents, Glucophage may be used as monotherapy or in combination with insulin.

items.t: Type 2 diabetes mellitus in adults (monotherapy, with other oral antidiabetics, or with insulin).

src.q: Glucophage SR may be used as monotherapy or in combination with other oral antidiabetic agents, or with insulin.

items.t: Reduction in risk or delay of onset of type 2 diabetes in overweight adults with IGT and/or IFG and/or raised HbA1c at high risk, still progressing despite 3 to 6 months of intensive lifestyle change.

src.q: Reduction in the risk or delay of the onset of type 2 diabetes mellitus in adult, overweight patients with IGT* and/or IFG*, and/or increased HbA1C

items.t: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS): ovulation stimulation to support conception.

src.q: Ovulation stimulation to support conception in women with PCOS.

items.t: Prediabetes indication: consider only where 3 to 6 months of intensive lifestyle change has not given adequate glycaemic control; treatment must be based on a risk score including evidence of high cardiovascular risk.

src.q: Metformin should only be considered where intensive lifestyle modifications for 3 to 6 months have not resulted in adequate glycaemic control.
Treatment with Glucophage SR must be based on a risk score incorporating appropriate measures of glycaemic control and including evidence of high cardiovascular risk

items.t: Switching from immediate-release metformin above 2000 mg daily to prolonged-release is not recommended.

src.q: In patients treated with metformin at a dose above 2000 mg daily, switching to Glucophage SR is not recommended.

items.t: Start 500 mg or 850 mg two or three times daily during or after meals. Adjust after 10 to 15 days by blood glucose; slow increase helps GI tolerance. Maximum 3 g daily in 3 divided doses (normal renal function, GFR ≥ 90 mL/min).
items.tag: Type 2 diabetes, adults: monotherapy or with other oral antidiabetics

src.q: The usual starting dose is 500 mg or 850 mg metformin hydrochloride 2 or 3 times daily given during or after meals. After 10 to 15 days the dose should be adjusted on the basis of blood glucose measurements.
A slow increase of dose may improve gastrointestinal tolerability.
The maximum recommended dose of metformin hydrochloride is 3 g daily, taken as 3 divided doses.

items.t: With insulin: usual starting dose 500 mg or 850 mg two or three times daily; insulin dose adjusted by blood glucose.

src.q: Metformin hydrochloride is given at the usual starting dose of 500 mg or 850 mg 2 or 3 times daily, while insulin dosage is adjusted on the basis of blood glucose measurements.

items.t: Start 500 mg once daily (with the evening meal). Increase by 500 mg every 10 to 15 days to a maximum of 2000 mg once daily with the evening meal. If not controlled, consider 1000 mg twice daily with food; if still not controlled, switch to standard tablets up to 3000 mg daily. Patients already on metformin: start at the equivalent daily dose.
items.tag: Type 2 diabetes, adults: monotherapy or with other oral antidiabetics

src.q: The usual starting dose is one tablet of Glucophage SR 500 mg once daily.
Dosage increases should be made in increments of 500mg every 10-15 days, up to a maximum of 2000mg once daily with the evening meal.
If glycaemic control is not achieved on Glucophage SR 2000mg once daily, Glucophage SR 1000mg twice daily should be considered, with both doses being given with food.
In patients already treated with metformin tablets, the starting dose of Glucophage SR should be equivalent to the daily dose of metformin immediate release tablets.

items.t: With insulin: usual start 500 mg once daily; insulin dose adjusted by blood glucose.

src.q: The usual starting dose of Glucophage SR is one 500 mg tablet once daily, while insulin dosage is adjusted on the basis of blood glucose measurements.

items.t: Start 500 mg once daily with the evening meal; adjust after 10 to 15 days. Maximum 2000 mg once daily with the evening meal. Review glycaemic status and risk factors every 3 to 6 months.
items.tag: Reduction in risk/delay of type 2 diabetes, adults

src.q: The therapy should be initiated with one tablet Glucophage SR 500 mg once daily with the evening meal.
The maximum recommended dose is 4 tablets (2000 mg) once daily with the evening meal.
It is recommended to regularly monitor (every 3-6 months) the glycaemic status

items.t: Usual dose 1500 to 2000 mg once daily; maximum 2000 mg once daily with the evening meal. Consider for at least 6 months.

src.q: The usual dose is 1,500-2000 mg once daily.
The maximum recommended dose is 2000 mg once daily with the evening meal. Glucophage SR should be considered for at least 6 months.

items.t: Elderly: adjust dose to renal function; assess renal function regularly.

src.q: Due to the potential for decreased renal function in elderly subjects, the metformin dosage should be adjusted based on renal function.

items.t: Children from 10 years and adolescents (type 2 diabetes): start 500 mg or 850 mg once daily during or after meals; adjust after 10 to 15 days. Maximum 2 g daily in 2 or 3 divided doses.

src.q: The usual starting dose is 500 mg or 850 mg metformin hydrochloride once daily, given during or after meals.
The maximum recommended dose of metformin hydrochloride is 2 g daily, taken as 2 or 3 divided doses.

items.t: Not licensed below 10 years (the SmPC licenses use from 10 years). Particular caution aged 10 to 12 years (few studied). Follow growth and puberty, especially before puberty. Confirm the diagnosis of type 2 diabetes before starting.

src.q: Glucophage can be used in children from 10 years of age and adolescents.
particular caution is recommended when prescribing to children aged between 10 and 12 years
a careful follow-up of the effect of metformin on these parameters in metformin-treated children, especially prepubescent children, is recommended
The diagnosis of type 2 diabetes mellitus should be confirmed before treatment with metformin is initiated.

items.t: Prolonged-release tablets should not be used in children (no data).

src.q: In the absence of available data, Glucophage SR should not be used in children.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to metformin or any excipient.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to metformin or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

items.t: Any acute metabolic acidosis (e.g. lactic acidosis, diabetic ketoacidosis); diabetic pre-coma.

src.q: Any type of acute metabolic acidosis (such as lactic acidosis, diabetic ketoacidosis). Diabetic pre-coma.

items.t: Severe renal failure (GFR < 30 mL/min).

src.q: Severe renal failure (GFR < 30 mL/min).

items.t: Acute conditions that may alter renal function: dehydration, severe infection, shock.

src.q: Acute conditions with the potential to alter renal function such as: dehydration, severe infection, shock.

items.t: Disease that may cause tissue hypoxia: decompensated heart failure, respiratory failure, recent myocardial infarction, shock.

src.q: Disease which may cause tissue hypoxia (especially acute disease, or worsening of chronic disease) such as: decompensated heart failure, respiratory failure, recent myocardial infarction, shock.

items.t: Hepatic insufficiency, acute alcohol intoxication, alcoholism.

src.q: Hepatic insufficiency, acute alcohol intoxication, alcoholism.

items.t: Lactic acidosis (very rare, serious): risk rises with acute worsening of renal function, cardiorespiratory illness or sepsis. Temporarily stop metformin in dehydration (severe diarrhoea or vomiting, fever, reduced fluid intake). Other risk factors: excess alcohol, hepatic insufficiency, poorly controlled diabetes, ketosis, prolonged fasting, hypoxia.

src.q: Lactic acidosis, a very rare, but serious metabolic complication, most often occurs at acute worsening of renal function or cardiorespiratory illness or sepsis.
In case of dehydration (severe diarrhoea or vomiting, fever or reduced fluid intake), metformin should be temporarily discontinued and contact with a health care professional is recommended.
Other risk factors for lactic acidosis are excessive alcohol intake, hepatic insufficiency, inadequately controlled diabetes, ketosis, prolonged fasting and any conditions associated with hypoxia

items.t: Iodinated contrast (intravascular): stop metformin before or at the time of imaging; do not restart until at least 48 hours after, and only when renal function has been re-checked and is stable.

src.q: Metformin should be discontinued prior to or at the time of the imaging procedure and not restarted until at least 48 hours after, provided that renal function has been re-evaluated and found to be stable

items.t: Surgery under general, spinal or epidural anaesthesia: stop metformin at the time of surgery; restart no earlier than 48 hours after surgery or resumption of oral nutrition, once renal function is re-checked and stable.

src.q: Metformin must be discontinued at the time of surgery under general, spinal or epidural anaesthesia.
Therapy may be restarted no earlier than 48 hours following surgery or resumption of oral nutrition and provided that renal function has been re-evaluated and found to be stable.

items.t: Heart failure: stable chronic heart failure - may be used with regular monitoring of cardiac and renal function. Acute and unstable heart failure - contraindicated.

src.q: In patients with stable chronic heart failure, metformin may be used with a regular monitoring of cardiac and renal function.
For patients with acute and unstable heart failure, metformin is contraindicated

items.t: Mitochondrial disease (MELAS, MIDD): metformin is not recommended; withdraw immediately if suggestive signs appear.

src.q: metformin is not recommended due to the risk of lactic acidosis exacerbation and neurologic complications which may lead to worsening of the disease

items.t: Medicines that can acutely impair renal function (antihypertensives, diuretics, NSAIDs) should be started with caution.

src.q: Medicinal products that can acutely impair renal function (such as antihypertensives, diuretics and NSAIDs) should be initiated with caution in metformin-treated patients.

items.t: Metformin alone does not cause hypoglycaemia; caution when combined with insulin or other oral antidiabetics (e.g. sulfonylureas, meglitinides).

src.q: Metformin alone does not cause hypoglycaemia, but caution is advised when it is used in combination with insulin or other oral antidiabetics (e.g. sulfonylureas or meglitinides).

items.t: Prediabetes indication: initiation not recommended at 75 years and older (benefit not established).

src.q: Due to the limited therapeutic efficacy data in the reduction of risk or delay of type 2 diabetes in patients 75 years and older, metformin initiation is not recommended in these patients.

items.t: Prolonged-release: tablet shells may appear in the faeces; this is normal.

src.q: The tablet shells may be present in the faeces. Patients should be advised that this is normal.

items.t: Prolonged-release in PCOS/premenopausal women: may cause ovulation in anovulatory women, which may lead to unintended pregnancy.

src.q: In premenopausal women, treatment with Glucophage SR may result in ovulation in anovulatory women, which may lead to unintended pregnancy.

items.t: Iodinated contrast agents: concomitant use not recommended - stop metformin before/at imaging, restart at least 48 hours after once renal function is stable.

src.q: Iodinated contrast agents Metformin must be discontinued prior to or at the time of the imaging procedure

items.t: Alcohol: not recommended - alcohol intoxication increases lactic acidosis risk, especially with fasting, malnutrition or hepatic impairment.

src.q: Alcohol intoxication is associated with an increased risk of lactic acidosis, particularly in case of fasting, malnutrition or hepatic impairment.

items.t: NSAIDs (including COX-2 inhibitors), ACE inhibitors, angiotensin II receptor antagonists and diuretics (especially loop diuretics): may impair renal function and raise lactic acidosis risk - close monitoring of renal function is necessary.

src.q: Some medicinal products can adversely affect renal function which may increase the risk of lactic acidosis, e.g. NSAIDs, including selective cyclo-oxygenase (COX) II inhibitors, ACE inhibitors, angiotensin II receptor antagonists and diuretics, especially loop diuretics.
When starting or using such products in combination with metformin, close monitoring of renal function is necessary.

items.t: Glucocorticoids (systemic and local) and sympathomimetics: more frequent blood glucose monitoring may be needed; adjust metformin dose if necessary.

src.q: Medicinal products with intrinsic hyperglycaemic activity (e.g. glucocorticoids (systemic and local routes) and sympathomimetics)
More frequent blood glucose monitoring may be required, especially at the beginning of treatment.

items.t: OCT2 inhibitors (e.g. trimethoprim, cimetidine, dolutegravir, ranolazine): may raise metformin levels - caution, especially in renal impairment; consider dose adjustment.

src.q: Inhibitors of OCT2 (such as cimetidine, dolutegravir, ranolazine, trimethoprim, vandetanib, isavuconazole) may decrease the renal elimination of metformin
Caution is therefore advised, especially in patients with renal impairment, when these drugs are co-administered with metformin, as metformin plasma concentration may increase.

items.t: Assess GFR before starting and at least annually; every 3 to 6 months in the elderly and those at risk of progression. The SmPC table uses GFR in mL/min.

src.q: A GFR should be assessed before initiation of treatment with metformin containing products and at least annually thereafter.
renal function should be assessed more frequently, e.g. every 3-6 months

items.t: GFR 60-89 mL/min: maximum 3000 mg/day (in 2-3 doses); dose reduction may be considered as renal function declines.

src.q: 60-89 3000 mg Dose reduction may be considered in relation to declining renal function.

items.t: BUMPS: metformin can be used in pregnancy to treat diabetes; no known risks to the baby. Use near delivery can cause short-lived low blood sugar in the newborn, so the baby's blood sugar is checked.

items.t: SmPC: metformin passes into breast milk; no adverse effects seen in breastfed infants, but data are limited so breastfeeding is not recommended during treatment. Decide whether to stop breastfeeding by weighing its benefit against the possible risk to the child.
